mathprize-olympiad-2019-01.title: Double counting by element degree
mathprize-olympiad-2019-01.body:
Let $S=\bigcup A_i$ and, for $x\in S$, let $\deg x$ be the number of indices $i$ with $x\in A_i$. Counting pairs $(i,x)$ with $x\in A_i$ and triples $(i,j,x)$ with $i<j$, $x\in A_i\cap A_j$:
$$\sum_i|A_i|=\sum_{x\in S}\deg x,\qquad\sum_{i<j}|A_i\cap A_j|=\sum_{x\in S}\binom{\deg x}2.$$

**Lemma.** For every integer $d$, $1\ge\frac d2-\frac16\binom d2$.

*Proof.* Since $d\le3$ or $d\ge4$, $(d-3)(d-4)\ge0$, i.e. $d^2-7d+12\ge0$, i.e. $12\ge7d-d^2=6d-d(d-1)$. Divide by $12$. $\square$

Apply the lemma to $d=\deg x$ for each $x\in S$ and add:
$$|S|=\sum_{x\in S}1\ge\frac12\sum_{x}\deg x-\frac16\sum_x\binom{\deg x}2=\frac12\sum_i|A_i|-\frac16\sum_{i<j}|A_i\cap A_j|.\ ∎$$

mathprize-olympiad-2019-02.title: Complex numbers
mathprize-olympiad-2019-02.body:
Place $A=0$, $B=1$, $C=\operatorname{cis}60^\circ=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$. Let $X=(1-t)B+tC$ with $t=BX\in[0,1]$:
$$X=p+qi,\qquad p=1-\tfrac t2,\quad q=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2t.$$

**Orientation.** Points $X,Y,Z$ on the sides $BC,CA,AB$, taken in this order, go around the boundary of the convex triangle counterclockwise (the same way as $A,B,C$), so triangle $XYZ$ is counterclockwise (a right isosceles triangle with $XY=XZ$ is non-degenerate). With the right angle at $X$ and $XY=XZ$, the vector $\overrightarrow{XZ}$ is $\overrightarrow{XY}$ rotated by $+90^\circ$:
$$Z-X=i(Y-X)\iff(1-i)X=Z-iY.$$

**Solving.** $Y$ lies on line $AC$, so $Y=r\operatorname{cis}60^\circ$ with $r$ real, and $Z=s$ with $s$ real (on line $AB$). Then
$$(1-i)X=(p+q)+(q-p)i,\qquad Z-iY=s-r\left(\tfrac{i}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)=\left(s+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2r\right)-\tfrac r2i.$$
Comparing parts: $-\frac r2=q-p$, so $r=2(p-q)$, and $s=p+q-\frac{\sqrt3}2r=(1-\sqrt3)p+(1+\sqrt3)q$. Substituting $p,q$:
$$r=2-(1+\sqrt3)t,\qquad s=1-\sqrt3+(1+\sqrt3)t.$$
So for each $X$ there is exactly one candidate pair $(Y,Z)$ on the lines, and $X$ is balanced iff $Y$ is on side $AC$ ($0\le r\le1$) and $Z$ is on side $AB$ ($0\le s\le1$).

- $0\le r\le1\iff\frac{\sqrt3-1}2\le t\le\sqrt3-1$.
- $0\le s\le1\iff2-\sqrt3\le t\le\frac{3-\sqrt3}2$.

Since $2-\sqrt3<\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$ and $\frac{3-\sqrt3}2<\sqrt3-1$, both hold exactly when
$$\frac{\sqrt3-1}2\le t\le\frac{3-\sqrt3}2.$$
The balanced points form this segment, of length $\frac{3-\sqrt3}2-\frac{\sqrt3-1}2=2-\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2-\sqrt3$.** ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2019-03.title: Length of an interval
mathprize-olympiad-2019-03.body:
**True.** It suffices to treat two consecutive red numbers $n^{2020}<(n+1)^{2020}$, both greater than $10^{10^8}$ (any two different red numbers have such a consecutive pair between or at them, and the blue numbers counted for different consecutive pairs lie in disjoint intervals). From $n^{2020}>10^{10^8}$ we get $n>10^{10^8/2020}>10^{10{,}000}$.

**Lemma.** If $x>10^{10{,}000}$, then $(x+1)^{2020/2019}>x^{2020/2019}+2019$.

*Proof.* $(x+1)^{2020/2019}=(x+1)(x+1)^{1/2019}>(x+1)x^{1/2019}=x^{2020/2019}+x^{1/2019}$, and $x^{1/2019}>10^{10{,}000/2019}>10^4>2019$. $\square$

By the lemma, the open interval $\left(n^{2020/2019},(n+1)^{2020/2019}\right)$ has length greater than $2019$, so it contains at least $2019$ integers $m$. For each, $m^{2019}$ lies strictly between $n^{2020}$ and $(n+1)^{2020}$, which are consecutive red numbers, so $m^{2019}$ is not red; being an $2019$-th power it is blue. The numbers $m^{2019}$ are distinct, so there are at least $2019$ blue integers between the two red ones. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2019-04.title: Induction with peeling lemmas
mathprize-olympiad-2019-04.body:
Write $a..b$ for $\{a,a+1,\dots,b\}$ (empty if $b<a$). An *$(n,c,d)$-partition* is a way to split $0..n$ into $c$ groups (empty groups allowed when the sum is $0$), each with element-sum $d$. Adding or removing the element $0$ does not change sums, and for $d\ge n\ge1$ the groups are nonempty, so the problem is equivalent to:

**Theorem.** If $n\ge1$, $d\ge n$, $c\ge1$ and $cd=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, there is an $(n,c,d)$-partition.

Three lemmas build bigger partitions from smaller ones.

**Lemma 1.** If $2c\le n+1$ and there is an $(n-2c,\,c,\,d-2n+2c-1)$-partition, there is an $(n,c,d)$-partition.
*Proof.* Split $n-2c+1..n$ into the $c$ pairs $\{n-2c+1+j,\ n-j\}$, $j=0,\dots,c-1$, each with sum $2n-2c+1$. Add one pair to each of the $c$ groups of the smaller partition; every group sum becomes $d$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** If $d$ is odd, $n\le d\le2n+1$, and there is a $(d-n-1,\ c-n+\frac{d-1}2,\ d)$-partition, there is an $(n,c,d)$-partition.
*Proof.* The set $d-n..n$ has $2n-d+1$ (even) elements and splits into the $n-\frac{d-1}2$ pairs $\{d-n+j,n-j\}$, each with sum $d$. Together with the given $c-n+\frac{d-1}2$ groups this gives $c$ groups of sum $d$ covering $0..d-n-1$ and $d-n..n$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** If $d$ is even, $n\le d\le2n$, and there is a $(d-n-1,\ 2c-2n+d-1,\ \frac d2)$-partition, there is an $(n,c,d)$-partition.
*Proof.* Note $d-n\le\frac d2\le n$. Add the singleton $\{\frac d2\}$ to the given partition: we get $2c-2n+d$ groups of sum $\frac d2$ covering $0..d-n-1$ and $\frac d2$; pair them up into $c-n+\frac d2$ groups of sum $d$. The remaining set $d-n..n$ minus $\frac d2$ splits into the $n-\frac d2$ pairs $\{d-n+j,n-j\}$, each with sum $d$. In total $c$ groups. $\square$

**Proof of the theorem** by strong induction on $n$. Note $\operatorname{sum}(1..m)=\frac{m(m+1)}2$.

1. *$d=n$.* Then $c=\frac{n+1}2$, and $(-1,c,0)$ (empty set, $c$ empty groups) is a partition. Lemma 1 gives $(n,c,d)$.
2. *$d=n+1$.* Then $c=\frac n2$, and $(0,c,0)$ is a partition ($\{0\}$ and empty groups). Lemma 1 with $n-2c=0$ and $d-2n+2c-1=0$ gives $(n,c,d)$.
3. *$n+1<d\le2n$, $d$ odd.* Put $n'=d-n-1$, $c'=c-n+\frac{d-1}2$. Then $1\le n'<n$, $d>n'$, and
$$c'd=cd-\Bigl(n-\tfrac{d-1}2\Bigr)d=\operatorname{sum}(1..n)-\operatorname{sum}(d-n..n)=\operatorname{sum}(1..n'),$$
so by induction an $(n',c',d)$-partition exists, and Lemma 2 gives $(n,c,d)$.
4. *$n+1<d\le2n$, $d$ even.* Put $n'=d-n-1$, $c'=2c-2n+d-1$, $d'=\frac d2$. Then $1\le n'<n$ and $d'>n'$ (as $d\le2n$). Since $\operatorname{sum}(d-n..n)=\left(n-\frac d2\right)d+\frac d2$,
$$c'd'=cd-nd+\tfrac{d^2}2-\tfrac d2=\operatorname{sum}(1..n)-\operatorname{sum}(d-n..n)=\operatorname{sum}(1..n').$$
By induction an $(n',c',d')$-partition exists, and Lemma 3 gives $(n,c,d)$.
5. *$d>2n$.* From $cd=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ we get $c<\frac{n+1}4$, so $4c\le n$. Put $n'=n-2c$, $d'=d-2n+2c-1$. Then $2c\le n'<n$, and since $\operatorname{sum}(n-2c+1..n)=c(2n-2c+1)$,
$$cd'=cd-c(2n-2c+1)=\operatorname{sum}(1..n').$$
Hence $d'=\frac{n'(n'+1)}{2c}\ge n'+1>n'$, so by induction an $(n',c,d')$-partition exists, and Lemma 1 (note $2c\le n+1$) gives $(n,c,d)$.

The cases cover all $d\ge n$. For $n=1$ only $d=1$ occurs (Case 1), so the base case needs no induction. Removing $0$ gives the required partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. ∎
